reason: The sources provide multi-site verified receipts confirming Chariklo's 2013-2014 ring discovery, physical dimensions, and occultation observations.
story: For centuries, astronomers assumed that ring systems were the exclusive glory of colossal gas giants like Saturn and Uranus. Small celestial rocks were thought far too tiny to hold onto a ring. But in June 2013, an international team led by astronomer Felipe Braga-Ribas watched a distant background star pass behind 10199 Chariklo, a 155-mile-wide centaur drifting beyond Saturn. They aimed only to measure the asteroid's size. Instead, seconds before and after the rock occulted the star, the starlight dipped twice in rapid succession. Chariklo was encircled by two dense, icy rings orbiting just 250 miles from its center. The discovery instantly solved a decade-long mystery: Chariklo had dimmed between 1997 and 2008 because its rings had turned edge-on to Earth. The tiny world proved that gargantuan gravity is not required to wear a crown of ice.
angle: Astronomers long believed only giant planets could possess dense rings, until a minor planet barely 155 miles wide was caught hiding two icy rings of its own.

claims.claim: 10199 Chariklo is classified as a centaur, a small Solar System body orbiting between the outer giant planets.
Chariklo orbits the Sun in the region between Saturn and Uranus.
Chariklo has an estimated mean diameter of approximately 250 kilometers (about 155 to 160 miles).
Chariklo is the largest known member of the centaur population.
Prior to Chariklo's discovery, rings had only been confirmed around giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
Astronomers discovered rings around Chariklo while observing a stellar occultation on June 3, 2013.
The discovery was publicly announced on March 26, 2014, and published in the journal Nature.
The observational campaign was led by Brazilian astronomer Felipe Braga-Ribas.
The occultation was observed using a network of telescopes across South America.
The 1.54-metre Danish National Telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile was among the participating instruments.
The occulted star was UCAC4 248-108672, located in the constellation Scorpius.
Astronomers identified the rings because the star's light blinked briefly several seconds before and after the main occultation by Chariklo.
Chariklo is encircled by two distinct, narrow rings.
The two rings have widths measured at approximately 7 kilometers and 3 kilometers.
The rings orbit at approximate distances of 391 kilometers and 405 kilometers from the center of Chariklo.
Chariklo became the first minor planet or asteroid-like body discovered to host its own ring system.
Spectroscopic measurements indicate the rings are composed at least partly of water ice.
Chariklo's observed dimming between 1997 and 2008 was caused by the rings tilting into an edge-on orientation toward Earth.
The gradual disappearance of water-ice absorption lines prior to 2008 matched the rings turning edge-on.
Without confinement, collisions between ring particles are expected to disperse the rings over time.
Astronomers hypothesize that small, undiscovered shepherd moons gravitationally shepherd and stabilize the rings.
The discovery team nicknamed the two rings Oiapoque and Chuí after border rivers in Brazil.

disputed: Number of observing sites: ESO (S3), Planetary Society (S5), and NatGeo (S6) mention telescopes at seven locations, while Wikipedia (S2) refers to ten telescopes and thirteen participating institutions/observatories. A script should refer generally to 'telescopes at multiple South American observatories' or specify 'seven successful observing sites.'

Ring dimensions: Nature (S4) and ESO (S3) report widths of about 7 km and 3 km separated by a 9 km gap, whereas Wikipedia (S1) gives the outer ring width as 0.12 km and a 14 km separation. A script should rely on the primary Nature/ESO peer-reviewed measurements.

Water ice location: Initial discovery reports (S2, S4) suggested the asteroid body was nearly devoid of water ice and that signatures came almost entirely from the rings, whereas later 2022 JWST data (S1) revealed crystalline water ice on Chariklo's surface itself. The script should attribute early conclusions to initial observations or note the updated JWST surface findings.
